blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A confounder is a variable that is associated with the exposure, is a cause of the outcome (or a proxy for one) through a route that does not pass through the exposure, and is not itself a consequence of the exposure. Its presence distorts the observed exposure–outcome association.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Return to ice cream and drowning. The arithmetic is right; the comparison is wrong. Comparing high-ice-cream days with low-ice-cream days is secretly comparing hot days with cold days. A comparison is clean only if the groups are alike in every other respect that affects the outcome. When they are not, the difference you measure mixes the effect you want with the effects of everything else that differed. That mixing is confounding.

Three conditions make a variable a confounder:

  1. It is associated with the exposure.
  2. It affects the outcome other than through the exposure.
  3. It is not on the causal path from the exposure to the outcome.

The third condition separates a confounder from two other kinds of third variable.

A mediator lies on the causal path: it is part of how the exposure acts. If maternal education improves child nutrition partly through better hygiene, hygiene is a mediator. Adjusting for it removes part of the effect you want to measure. This error is overadjustment.

A collider is caused by two variables on a path, for example by both the exposure and the outcome. Adjusting for a collider, or selecting study participants on it, creates an association that was not there. Variables measured after the exposure and outcome, or plausibly caused by them, are not automatically safe to adjust for.

Which variables belong in an analysis is therefore a question about how the variables are related in the world. The data cannot tell a cause from an effect. That judgement comes from subject knowledge and must be made before the analysis, not discovered during it.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
A survey finds that households owning a radio have better-nourished children. Three candidate third variables:

  • Household wealth. Wealthier households are more likely to own a radio (condition 1), feed their children better for reasons that have nothing to do with the radio (condition 2), and do not become wealthy because they own a radio (condition 3). Wealth is a confounder. Ignoring it overstates the benefit of the radio.
  • Exposure to nutrition messages. If the radio delivers feeding advice that improves nutrition, the messages lie on the path from radio to nutrition. They are a mediator. Adjusting for them would hide a real effect.
  • Enrolment in a nutrition programme. If radio-owning households hear about the programme and better-nourished children’s families are more likely to stay enrolled, enrolment is caused by both. It is a collider. Studying only enrolled households would distort the radio–nutrition association.

Three variables, each correlated with both radio ownership and nutrition, need three different decisions.

blocks.alt: Confounder, mediator, and collider as causal diagrams
blocks.caption: Figure 11.3. Confounder, mediator and collider as causal diagrams. X is the exposure, Y the outcome and Z the third variable.

points.html: Confounder: adjust for it. Mediator: do not, if you want the total effect of the exposure. Collider: do not. Correlations alone cannot tell you which is which.

Confounding reflects how variables are related in the population, not an error in how the study was run. That is why a measured confounder can be dealt with at the analysis stage: by stratification (§11.7), by standardisation (recall §7.4.2) or by regression (§12.4.1, multiple regression).
Unmeasured confounding comes from a confounder that was never recorded. No analysis of the data at hand can remove it.

Residual confounding is what remains after adjusting for a measured confounder, because it was measured with error or grouped too coarsely (for example, wealth recorded as just “poor/not poor”) (Fewell et al., 2007; Tripepi et al., 2010). The two are different problems: residual confounding can shrink with better measurement or finer strata; unmeasured confounding cannot shrink without new data.
Chapter 17 (§17.3) returns to confounding as a threat to validity and to what study design can do about it.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A causal diagram, or directed acyclic graph (DAG), draws each variable as a node and each assumed direct cause as an arrow from cause to effect. “Directed” means every arrow has one direction; “acyclic” means you can never follow arrows back to where you started.

  • A path is any route between two nodes along arrows, whatever their direction, that passes through no node more than once.
  • A causal path from exposure E to outcome W follows arrows forwards all the way (E → … → W).
  • A backdoor path is a path from E to W that starts with an arrow into E (E ← …). An open backdoor path carries confounding.
  • On a path, a node where two arrowheads meet (→ C ←) is a collider on that path.
  • A descendant of E is any node you can reach from E by following arrows forwards (in Figure 11.4 below: A, P, H and W).
  • A path is open (transmits association) unless it is blocked. It is blocked if it contains a non-collider that you adjust for, or a collider that you do not adjust for (and none of whose descendants you adjust for).

The backdoor criterion: a set of variables Z is sufficient to remove confounding of the effect of E on W if (1) no variable in Z is a descendant of E, and (2) Z blocks every backdoor path from E to W (Greenland, Pearl & Robins, 1999). A minimal adjustment set is a sufficient set from which no variable can be removed.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Association flows along open paths like water through pipes. The causal paths carry the effect you want. The backdoor paths carry confounding. Adjusting for a variable in the middle of a pipe closes it. A collider is a pipe that is closed until you adjust for it; adjusting opens it. So the job is: keep the causal paths untouched, close every backdoor path, and open no collider. The diagram makes the job mechanical once you have drawn it; the hard part is drawing it honestly from subject knowledge.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Does maternal education (E) raise birthweight (W)? Figure 11.4 records the assumptions of a hypothetical study team.

blocks.alt: A causal diagram for maternal education and birthweight
blocks.caption: Figure 11.4. Assumed causal structure. Household socioeconomic status (S) affects education, antenatal care (A) and birthweight. Education acts on birthweight directly and through ANC visits and parity (P). Hospital delivery (H) is affected by education and by pregnancy complications (C), which also lower birthweight.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. List every path from E to W (seven in all):
    • E → W; E → A → W; E → P → W (causal paths)
    • E ← S → W; E ← S → A → W (backdoor paths)
    • E → A ← S → W; E → H ← C → W (non-causal paths that start forwards; each contains a collider, A or H)
  2. With no adjustment, the three causal paths and the two backdoor paths are open. The two paths through a collider are blocked.
  3. Both backdoor paths pass through S. Adjusting for S blocks both. S is not a descendant of E. So {S} satisfies the backdoor criterion, and nothing can be removed from it: {S} is the minimal adjustment set for the total effect of education.
  4. Adjusting for A (ANC) instead is wrong twice. A is a mediator, so the path E → A → W is cut and part of the effect is lost. A is also a collider on E → A ← S → W, so adjusting for it opens that path; with S left unadjusted, a non-causal association flows through it.
  5. Restricting the study to hospital deliveries (conditioning on H) opens E → H ← C → W. Among hospital births, less-educated mothers are more likely to be there because of a complication, and complications lower birthweight. A spurious association appears even after adjusting for S. This is selection bias with a collider structure (Hernán et al., 2004).
  6. Parity (P) is a mediator here: adjust for it only if you want the effect of education other than through family size.

The free browser tool DAGitty (dagitty.net), “a browser-based environment for creating, editing, and analyzing causal diagrams”, lists the paths and minimal adjustment sets for larger diagrams.

points.html: A DAG is a statement of assumptions, not a finding. Two teams can draw different diagrams; the diagram makes the disagreement visible and checkable.
The traditional three-condition test of §11.6 can mislead when there are several possible confounders; the backdoor criterion corrects it (Greenland, Pearl & Robins, 1999).
Do not adjust for a descendant of the exposure when estimating its total effect (condition 1 of the backdoor criterion).
An arrow you leave out is a strong claim: it says there is no direct effect.
Hernán et al. (2004) show that many selection biases have the same structure: conditioning on a common effect (a collider). Chapter 17 (§17.2) uses this.

questions.prompt: In the district example of §11.5 (more health workers, more recorded disease), name one explanation of each of the four kinds (chance, bias, confounding, reverse causation).
questions.answer:
• Chance: with few districts, or after checking many indicators, a correlation can arise by accident; the p-value and CI address this.
  • Bias (information bias): more health workers find and record more cases, so recorded disease rises with staffing even if true disease does not.
  • Confounding: population size (or urbanisation) raises both the number of posts and the number of cases.
  • Reverse causation: districts with a heavy disease burden are sent more health workers.

questions.prompt: In Figure 11.4, how many paths join E and W, and how many of them are backdoor paths? A colleague adjusts for ANC visits and analyses only hospital deliveries. Which non-causal paths does she open? What should she adjust for instead?
questions.answer:
1. Seven paths: E → W, E → A → W, E → P → W (causal); E ← S → W, E ← S → A → W (two backdoor paths); E → A ← S → W and E → H ← C → W (non-causal, each blocked by a collider).
  2. Adjusting for A (a collider on E → A ← S → W) opens that path; since she has not adjusted for S, a non-causal association runs from E through A and S to W. It also cuts the causal path E → A → W (overadjustment). Restricting to hospital deliveries conditions on H and opens E → H ← C → W (collider/selection bias).
  3. She should adjust for S alone, the minimal adjustment set, and study all births, not only hospital births.

questions.prompt: Wealth is recorded only as “above or below the poverty line”. After adjusting for it, the radio–nutrition association shrinks but does not vanish. Is what remains unmeasured or residual confounding? What would reduce it?
questions.answer: It is (at least partly) residual confounding: wealth was measured and adjusted for, but a two-category measure leaves large wealth differences within each category. Measuring wealth more finely (an asset index in quintiles, or as a continuous score) and adjusting for that would reduce it. Any confounder that was never recorded (for example, the mother’s own interest in health information) would be unmeasured confounding, which better use of the existing data cannot remove.
